Back when I was under the influence of religion (from a young age through my twenties) I gave it a serious go. It was just such a hard read I never got that far. I'd try skipping to the next book to see how it struck me. Nothing really read well. There are a few cool names of angels, demons, kings and whatnot, but that's about all I can say for it...

Most attempts get stuck in the books after exodous (Leviticus through Deuteronomy) which is too bad because the narrative form is preserved for most of the remaining books (with a long break for poetry).

Slate has a series years ago following a read through the Jewish bible. I enjoyed reading it (and recall the comments being better than typical).

I think the bible is useful in understanding European/christian art and literature. The symbolism makes a lot more sense after you've read it.

A second benefit of the bible is that it kickstarted textual criticism, which is to combine various sources of one work and to work out with some confidence what it is most likely to have been as written by the original author. This has since been used successfully to reconstruct other works even though nothing has as many complete books and fragments as the bible itself.

That concludes how useful it is, though.

What I mostly got from it is a clear sense that the god described in it is dishonourable, uncaring towards those devoted to him, and extremely aggressive towards perpetrators of even minor offenses against his majesty.

Some parts are written well, some parts poorly. It's evident there's a lot of different authors, writing in hugely different styles.

The morality which is assumed by the authors places men above women without even questioning that premise, and a thin veneer of "god said so" is slapped onto it. This likely is meant to show how wise this god is, keeping the wymyns in their place. The same is true for parents over children, and kings over subjects.

Little things like how Job is rewarded with a new batch of kids as if that means it's okay that the other kids were killed, or how a psalm speaks joyfully of smashing the heads of conquered little children, or how women are unfit to teach men, or how the new testament generally skirts around the question if Jesus is god or not (he is tho, just trying for some plausible deniability in case people want to enforce that taboo), and many other such examples thoroughly clarified that my sense of morality didn't match the biblical one at all.

I'd say it was interesting, but if I had to write an unbiased book review, I would call it the single most overrated book in the history of human literature.

I also (foolishly) tried to go one step deeper, and look at the original text. I've got a mild case of history nerdism, so it wasn't like I had to force myself too hard. I did a few random pages of interest in literal translation, and it just sounded completely appropriate for its historical context, and completely irrelevant for today. Some small details like how the commandment is actually "thou shalt not murder" (as in no killing unless it's legal, and we'll tell you when this is!) became clearer, but it didn't improve my overall impression of the story.

Trying to pretend this work is relevant two thousand years (or more, since some parts are far older) later is just stupid. There's nothing mysterious or unique in there, and it clearly reflects the worldview of people in the general area of what is now mostly Israel at the time of writing. There is no sign of unexpected outside knowledge enriching the authors.

It really destroyed the last vestiges of doubt I had about whether there is something in there to call divinely inspired. So much so that I would encourage any christian to read every single word of the bible, to help them see what a massive crock of shit they're holding sacred.

I didn't like the Bible. For the same reason that I don't generally like cheap B-movies. It's boring, it drags on, and it's irrelevant in today's society. Everyone will say that it's necessary to understand culture and nuance today. Not so, no more than it is to understand culture and nuance through rap music which influences ebonics, or celebrity culture which influences vernacular. It's only relevant if you associate in those types of groups. And I would prefer not to associate with anyone who sees the Bible as a moral guide. It's just a bad book to me. And not bad in the sense of morally bad, bad in the sense of aesthetics. None of the stories make any sense. People in them are one-sided and and have foolish motives, and everyone is generally an idiot/psychopath with no sense of morality. (Immoral with a god, hmm, wonder how that works)

I liked Genesis and some of the other books. Some parts were outright boring, like describing minute mundane details of building an altar. What I found most surprising was the lack of wisdom contained in the pages. There was some very common sense verses in Proverbs, but beyond that, not much enlightenment at all.

As a young man I did read the bible, king James version, cover to cover twice. I did not enjoy it either time. The second read of the Bible was to be sure I really didn't like it and that I was sure I couldn't justify the contradictions to sustain my belief as I was heading toward my current belief, that being, I don't believe. I have also read the Qur'on, Book of Mormon, Egyptian Book of the Dead, the writings of Alister Crowley, and another large religious tome whose name I don't recall at the moment. All crap. I simply do not believe that any true followers of any religion has bothered to read the books that they profess as their life guide and basis of their belief. To read the complete bible then close the cover and pronounce that one 'believes' what they have just read is, in my opinion (which I am entitled to), is insanity.

When I was also under the influence of religion, I did read it. And the Book of Mormon. And Jesus the Christ by Talmage. Multiple times.

The OT was meh. Psalms was enjoyable for its poetry. The NT was okay.

Yeah, I was Mormon.

Back in 10th grade my drum instructor wanted me to join him to bible study. He ended up convincing me to read the bible, and if I could pass a test he designed about the bible, he would give me $100. I read the bible, passed the test, and continued going to bible studies with him just so I could question the issues I had with the bible and it's inconsistancies. He was a great guy though, so I really did try to remain respectful. His friends were nice, we went paintballing one time as a bible study group. It was really cool.

I'm not religious, I think the bible is a great work of total fiction that should not be the base of any religion at all. In terms of originality, and hell even some morals aren't entirely terrible, it's just great fiction. Revelations, is probably the coolest story I've ever read in my entire life. Angels blaring horns, 4 horseman coming down raining death and horror on the planet. A woman giving birth in the sky only to have her baby eaten by a giant sky dragon. Locust with Womens head, lions teeth, and crazy demon tails. That shit would make a great sci fi movie.

Just wait until you get to ten strait chapters on how to build churches, and what kind of incense to wear, and what to eat, etc. etc.

The first bit is pretty good compared to the rest, then there is a metric fuck ton of grocery lists, a couple of acid trips, Jesus 4x, Peter telling everyone how he was Christian before it was cool, then some anti-roman propaganda written in code that has half of our congress trying to bring forth a seven headed dragon for Jesus to fight.

The underlying theme is that Humanity just can't do things right so they're always at fault, but there's a solution: stop questioning, stop thinking, stop taking care of your businesses because everything is gonna end soon and you're going to a place with no suffering, responsibility or dissent.
